title: Please Please Please
lyric_access: full (paraphrase only): the fetch tool read the whole lyric as printed by TODAY.com (SP-S1, a press article, not an official presentation, licence not stated) and returned a section map, line counts and paraphrase; I never saw the raw lyric. Song Exploder's transcript (AA-S2) prints many short sung excerpts, also seen only through tool extraction. The licensed display tried (Musixmatch, SP-S2) was blocked. Paraphrases of the bridge differed between extractions, so bridge detail is kept general.
angle: Subject label: a woman asking her partner not to misbehave. Actual angle: a vanity confession played for laughs. She can survive heartbreak but not public embarrassment, and says so. The title is the politest possible word tripled; the song's argument is that her pride, having vouched for him, is what is on the line.
narrator: First person, addressing one man who is present in the scene (an actor with a bad streak, by verse 1's pun). She is confident about her own taste yet pleading, and Antonoff says he felt sorry for her and scared of her. Meaningful ambiguity: the chorus's first line is presented in official materials both as him proving 'them' right and as him proving 'her' right (SP-S1; AA-S2 prints the first-person form), so she is either defending him against doubters or dreading confirmation of her own suspicion. Carpenter also calls it a conversation with herself (AA-F3).

section_map.function: Guitar riff before the voice; Carpenter calls it the kind of hook that tells you a favourite song is starting; Antonoff places it between singer-songwriter country and a band in a bar.

Establishes her credibility and her exposure: she insists her judgment and taste are good, concedes she is alone in thinking so, says she has vouched for him, and asks him (via a pun on his acting) to perform decency and keep his worst self in for the night. Sets up public stakes before the plea.
A single short direct line telling him she is asking one thing; pure hand-over to the chorus. Section label is the tool's inference; Song Exploder never names a pre-chorus.

The plea in descending register: polite tripled title, a petty stake (just did her makeup), a ranking of heartbreak below ego, a plain beg not to embarrass her, ending on the profane word. Carpenter says this passage was the most deliberately shaped, from something she said that day.

Daydream: stay in, keep the relationship hidden, then call it a joke (Carpenter: a little truth in it). Antonoff moves this verse from A to C so it sounds suspended; written by Carpenter and Allen in about five minutes while he changed key.
Same words as chorus 1 in the press print; Antonoff describes the drop back to A as popping the bubble, putting her back at the table pleading. Exact key sequence ambiguous in the extract.

Added about a month after the first session at Antonoff's LA studio. A sincere instruction to keep his foolishness away from her, followed straight away by a joke that turns it into a threat of lasting resentment. Both writers say they had said versions of these lines to real people.
The title plea repeated with stacked vocals, collapsing into bare pleading with the consequences dropped.

title_hook: The title opens the chorus and recurs about nine times in the press print, mostly inside the chorus and outro (approximate, tool count). It arrived first: Carpenter had the phrase before the song had a subject, matched to Antonoff's chorus chords (AA-F1). The meaning is not delayed so much as qualified: the polite word stays polite, and the edge comes at the end of each chorus rather than in the title. Antonoff hears the repetition as pleading; no source calls it a warning. Sound claims: none beyond the writers' statement that the chorus's last note was pushed low.

language_choices.what_it_does: The politest word in the language, repeated, becomes desperation; it keeps the hook radio-safe and lets the chorus spend its bluntness elsewhere.
Asks him only to perform decency, which is both a joke about his profession and a low-expectations insult; Carpenter says she sang the phrase on instinct against Antonoff's guitar.
A small, checkable, petty reason not to cry; it makes the tears comic and tells us she is vain and knows it.
A plain ranking line that splits private hurt from public pride and admits which one she cares about more; the song's angle in four words.
The bluntest word sits last in the chorus; the writers say it came as an ad lib with the melody pushed lower, and Allen says the room laughed and kept it.
No metaphor anywhere in the chorus; Antonoff says many lines were literal things Carpenter said. Plainness is stronger here because the comedy is in the ranking, not in the imagery.

connective_lines: Verse 1 is mostly connective: the concession that only she trusts her taste and the line saying she has vouched for him carry no punchline but create the public stakes the chorus needs. The one-line pre-chorus is purely functional, a plain ask that hands over to the plea. The punchlines (actor pun, makeup, the profane word) are spaced, not stacked.
musical: Documented (Antonoff, AA-S2, text-only): chorus chords came first; song starts in A, verse 2 moves to C, a modulation he describes as unnatural, for the fantasy, and the return to A pops the bubble; a steady LinnDrum against looser live drums and guitar; some guitar notes deliberately slightly out of tune against a pitch-perfect vocal; synths meant to sound like someone struggling with a new 1970s instrument; stacked vocals on the outro. Documented (Carpenter, AA-S2): one first-verse note change was a spontaneous reaction to the guitar; the chorus ending was moved from high to low. Press (via AA-S18): key change on the second verse (Evening Standard; NYT 2024-06-07); genre labels range from country pop to yacht rock, disco-pop and synth-pop across outlets. Text-only boundary: nothing here was checked against the recording.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sabrina Carpenter
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The song came from a period of swinging between confidence and desperation over men; it was funny to the writers and a way to be candid about embarrassment.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sabrina Carpenter
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Antonoff played the chorus chords first; she already had the title phrase before she knew what the song was about.

writer_commentary.speaker: Jack Antonoff
writer_commentary.paraphrase: He felt sorry for the narrator and scared of her; he often draws on a Dolly Parton tone that is sad but not to be messed with.

writer_commentary.speaker: Jack Antonoff
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Verse 2 moves from A to C to put the fantasy somewhere suspended; coming back to A pops the bubble.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sabrina Carpenter
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The heartbreak/ego/embarrassment passage was the most deliberately shaped part, from something she said that day; the melody ending was pushed lower and the profane word came as an ad lib. She and Allen wrote verse 2 in about five minutes while Antonoff changed key.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sabrina Carpenter
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The second-verse backing vocals are playful and include Amy Allen laughing, which adds truth to the joke.

writer_commentary.speaker: Jack Antonoff and Sabrina Carpenter
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The bridge was missing after day one and finished about a month later in LA; Antonoff was anxious because the song felt fragile. Its lines come from things both had said to people; the sincere line followed by the funny one makes the sad line hit harder.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sabrina Carpenter
writer_commentary.paraphrase: It is about a woman who knows she is heading for trouble and owns it; she calls it nearly autobiographical.

writer_commentary.speaker: Amy Allen
writer_commentary.paraphrase: When a line feels like it is pushing too far it is often the best part; the profane word in this song was laughed at, kept, and is now what people latch on to.

analyst_inference: The chorus enacts Carpenter's stated sweet-then-blunt preference as a fixed order of lines (SP-F3).
The angle is a ranked confession: pride above heartbreak (SP-F4).
The verse-2 wish to hide the relationship is the comic logical answer to the fear of public embarrassment (SP-F7).
The pronoun variance ('em vs I'm) holds two fears in one line (SP-F5).
revisions: Partly documented, no before/after wording. The chorus melody ending was moved from higher to lower during writing, and the profane final word arrived then as an ad lib (AA-S2). The bridge did not exist after the first session and was added about a month later (AA-S2). No discarded lyric lines are documented.

transferable.craft: Order a comic plea chorus from politest to bluntest: courteous title, one petty stake, a ranking line, the bluntest word last.
transferable.limits: Turns aggressive in a sincere or grieving song; as a habit it becomes the shtick critics punished on Man's Best Friend (AA-S21).

transferable.craft: Find the angle by asking what the narrator is most afraid of, and let her admit the petty fear outranks the noble one.
transferable.limits: Trivialises real loss; needs a narrator the audience already likes.

transferable.craft: Set a daydream section apart (key, register or texture) so the return to the chorus sounds like waking up.
transferable.limits: Musical claim from a writer statement only; without a real fantasy in the words the shift is a gimmick.

transferable.craft: Let the narrator state a wish and retract it as a joke, so the wish stays standing.
transferable.limits: Fails if the retraction crowds out the wish or if every wish is retracted.

exercise: Synthetic, not modelled on this song's lines: a narrator is bringing a new partner to her sister's wedding. Write a four-line chorus in which line 1 is the politest request she could make, line 2 a small, checkable, petty stake (something she spent money or time on), line 3 a ranking of two harms where the pettier one wins, and line 4 the bluntest thing she would really say, as the last word. Then write a flat version where all four lines sit at the same politeness level and compare which one has a payoff.

Song Exploder was read only through tool extraction; extractions disagreed on the bridge's joke detail and on which section returns to A. Allen does not speak in the episode, and no source says which co-writer wrote which line beyond verse 2 (Carpenter and Allen). No discarded drafts. No audio.

title: Ain't In LA
lyric_access: full (paraphrase only): Capital FM's article (AD-S18) prints the whole lyric with section labels, including intro and refrain labelled as Theron Thomas's; the fetch tool read it and returned a section map, line counts and line-by-line paraphrase, never the raw text. Press article, licence not stated, not an official presentation. Tool paraphrases disagreed on whether the pre-chorus presents leaving home as a taught belief or her own urge, and one Singles Jukebox critic mentions a line (learning English on a night shift) that the tool did not find in the print, so the print or the critic may be off. Songfacts (AD-S13) and Singles Jukebox (AD-S36) describe further lines.
angle: Subject label: hometown pride, you don't need LA. Actual angle: a daughter's tribute to her mother's unrecognised dreams, turned outward into an address to girls everywhere, and an LA resident refusing the city's claim to own cool rather than attacking the city. The title says only where the best people are not; where they are is left for the listener to supply.
narrator: Starts as a storyteller describing a girl in third person (inspired by her mother at 18; W's writer says verse 1 describes her mother's childhood), turns to 'you' in the second pre-chorus and verse 2, and first says 'I' in the chorus as an advocate; verse 2 ends on a first-person value claim. A second voice (Thomas) speaks without any 'I'. Ambiguities: the singer left home for LA while telling others they need not run away, and the chorus hedges ('maybe tonight'); the verse-1 girl's posters span acts roughly fifteen years apart, so she may be a composite rather than strictly the mother (my inference).

section_map.function: Second voice (labelled Theron Thomas; press: pitched-down, chopped and screwed) lists status images with no first person: tooth gems, trunk subwoofers, a modest car spinning in the rain. Sets up a world of flash for the chorus to answer.

Third-person inventory of a girl at home: shared room with a younger brother, hand-me-downs she customises, two named pop acts on her wall. No pity adjectives; Songfacts reads the details as style, not hardship.
The girl's self-belief (she knows she is beautiful and was raised to) and dreams that reach beyond home; builds the urge to leave that the chorus answers.
First 'I'. A hedged invitation not to run away tonight; calls LA's claim on the best people a lie; title closes line 2 and line 4, so the chorus ends on the rejected place.
Thomas's status-image block returns; stands in for any bridge as the song's only contrasting voice.
Widens from one girl to girls in unknown cities, tells 'you' you are one of a kind, ends with a first-person preference for being nobody over being like everyone. The move from portrait to crowd.
Same lines as pre-chorus 1, with 'she' turned to 'you'; the listener now stands where the girl stood.
Exact repeat; refrain adds an ad lib.
Chorus fragment ending on the title, so the song's last word is the place it rejects. No bridge anywhere.

title_hook: Vernacular negation ('ain't') in the title; it ends the chorus and its second line, and the outro ends on it, so LA is said most often and always denied. Delayed meaning: the title never says where the best people are; verse 1's unnamed bedroom and verse 2's unknown cities fill the gap without naming it. Listeners completed the slot with their own hometowns (AD-S18 para 8) and Vogue CS completed it in a headline (AD-S37). Sound: text-only, no claim.

language_choices.what_it_does: A vernacular negation gives the title attitude and defines worth by absence rather than by naming a rival place.
Plain nouns with no adjectives of pity let the girl's resourcefulness show; plainness is stronger than describing her as poor or brave.

language_choices.choice: two named pop acts on the wall
language_choices.what_it_does: The only proper nouns in the verses; they place the girl in pop history and connect to the smuggled-posters story ADÉLA tells (SP-S8). They span two eras, which loosens the portrait into a composite (my inference).
Softens the instruction not to leave, which matters because the singer did leave; without it the chorus would read as a lecture (my inference).
The narrator's own credo arrives late, after the portrait and the address; critics split on it (Gaze rejected it as a proverb, AD-S36).

language_choices.choice: Honda Civic among the refrain's flash images
language_choices.what_it_does: A modest car beside tooth gems and subwoofers; read as provincial cool it supports the chorus, read as glamour it contradicts it. Low-confidence inference.

connective_lines: The pre-chorus is the hinge: it carries no image, only the girl's self-belief and the urge outward, so the chorus has something to answer. Verse 1 is all connective detail with no punchline. The second pre-chorus's switch from 'she' to 'you' does the song's main structural work with one word.
musical: Press descriptions only, labelled: label copy describes booming 808s, glitchy drums and chopped-and-screwed vocals (SP-S8); W says Thomas raps the distorted refrain (AD-S10 para 9); Songfacts calls the intro chopped and screwed and an echo of We Can't Stop, which Thomas co-wrote (AD-S13); the FADER heard a pitched-down sample in the vein of early A$AP Rocky and Bangerz-era Miley (AD-S9). Songfacts relays ADÉLA, via a Billboard Chartbreaker interview it did not link, saying she wanted to bring back the 2010s sound. Singles Jukebox critics heard menacing sonics against hopeful lyrics (Davidson) and a nostalgic sound undercutting the outsider theme (Beardslee). Text-only boundary: nothing checked against the recording.

writer_commentary.speaker: ADÉLA
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Inspired by photos of her mother at 18 in front of pop posters her grandfather smuggled in from Germany; written for her mother and young women whose dreams may never be recognised.

writer_commentary.speaker: ADÉLA
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Lorde's Royals and Team meant a lot to her as a child and she wanted to write about being outside the zeitgeist; she lives in LA and is tired of the same people and beauty standards being praised; she will never be as cool as a girl far away who never got the chance.

writer_commentary.speaker: ADÉLA
writer_commentary.paraphrase: LA is a metaphor for something bigger; she was tired of songs celebrating celebrity culture; the song is for everyone, saying you need not come from a big city.

writer_commentary.speaker: ADÉLA
writer_commentary.paraphrase: You don't have to leave your country to find value in where you're from; American pop culture makes people feel they are missing a dream life elsewhere.

writer_commentary.speaker: ADÉLA (relayed from a live show, 2026-05-15 per Songfacts)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: She has lived in LA four years and loves it; the city's character comes from immigrants and people from other states.

writer_commentary.speaker: ADÉLA (relayed by Songfacts from an unlinked Billboard Chartbreaker interview)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The 2010s sound excited her and the team wanted to bring it back.

analyst_inference: The pronoun ladder (she, then you, then I) turns a tribute into an anthem without the singer making herself the subject (SP-F8).
The title's blank is the participation hook and the source of the critics' vagueness complaint (SP-F10).
The 'maybe' hedge keeps a stay-home message from contradicting a singer who left.
The verse-1 posters span eras, so the girl reads as a composite of mother and listener.
revisions: None documented. Jessica Doyle (AD-S36) speculates that an earlier draft named Bratislava; that is a critic's guess, not evidence. The only co-writer source located (Billboard on Theron Thomas, SP-S6) could not be read.

transferable.craft: For a tribute-turned-anthem, write verse 1 as a third-person portrait, switch the repeated pre-chorus from 'she' to 'you' the second time, and hold the narrator's 'I' for the chorus.
transferable.limits: Needs a concrete portrait; a thin one makes the 'you' address sound like a motivational poster (St. Asaph, AD-S36).

transferable.craft: Title a place song with the famous place it rejects and leave the affirmed place unnamed, deciding on purpose whether the blank is the point.
transferable.limits: Costs specificity; if the song honours one real town, name it (and compare C41).

transferable.craft: Hedge advice the singer has not followed ('maybe'), so the chorus invites rather than lectures.
transferable.limits: Analyst inference; a hedge in a defiant song can sound like loss of nerve.

transferable.craft: Use a second voice to state the world the chorus answers, in place of a bridge.
transferable.limits: If its imagery does not clearly belong to the world being refused, critics hear it as disconnected (Axelrod, AD-S36).

exercise: Synthetic: pick someone you love at fifteen. Verse 1: four plain nouns from their room or clothes, third person, no adjectives of pity. Pre-chorus: what they believed about themselves. title: Someone You Loved
lyric_access: partial: no full lyric seen. The licensed displays (Musixmatch SB-S18, LyricFind SB-S19) are blocked; the official site (SB-S17), the label release (SB-S16) and the label-owned Vevo Footnotes write-up (SB-S15) show none, and the Footnotes video, where Capaldi annotates lines, is not readable as text. What was legitimately visible: Plugged In's section-by-section paraphrase of the lyric, including three quoted words (SB-S10); critics' characterisations (SB-S9, SB-S11); and the writers' statements about scope and structure (SB-S3, SB-S5, SB-S7, SB-S8). Every lyric observation below is marked press, writer_statement or inferred.
angle: The subject label is heartbreak after a partner leaves. The angle is narrower: the loss shows how far the narrator had come to depend on being loved, and the title defines him only as the object of someone else's past love ('someone you loved', not 'someone I loved'). Capaldi says the scope was widened on purpose, from one old relationship to losing someone in general, so the absence can be read as a partner leaving or a relative dying (SB-S3#Q2; SB-S5#P7-P9). His own later accounts have named his grandmother, two family bereavements, and a fear of opening up in a new relationship (SB-S1#Background; SB-S13#para 4; SB-S6#fact 1).
narrator: First person, speaking to an absent 'you'. In the press paraphrase his stance is admission rather than accusation: he lists what he needs, owns having let his guard down and come to rely on being loved, and comforts himself with memory (SB-S10#'Wishing You Were Here' paras 1-3). The central ambiguity is why the 'you' is gone. Plugged In reads only a breakup (and reads one 'all or nothing' line as sexual), so the bereavement reading comes from interviews, not from anything the reviewer saw in the words; Kelleher says death was never mentioned in the session (SB-S8#Emotive Force ¶3). Blame is present (the other person pulled away) but carries less weight than the narrator's own exposure.

section_map.function: States the narrator's need in general terms (someone to heal, know and hold him), with no scene, place or event. The melody was Capaldi's: saved on his phone from band chords (NME), or improvised at the piano in the session (SOS)
Melodic ramp into the chorus. Capaldi and Barnes both credit the melody to Capaldi. Its lyric is not legitimately visible, so its verbal function is unverified

The admission: he had lowered his guard and come to depend on being loved, and the other person has gone; the title phrase is the object of that admission. Stereogum finds its framing of grief oddly blunt. Written on day one
section_map.basis: press (SB-S10#para 2; SB-S9#para 6) + writer_statement (SB-S8#Emotive Force ¶3); title placement inferred

section_map.function: Written about a week after the first session. The press paraphrase's material on getting by on memory and imagining being held may belong here or to the middle eight; placement not verifiable
Written in the second session. It is the only section with strings: a fuller string arrangement clouded the track and was cut back. Lyric not legitimately visible
Return of the admission; press describes the vocal pushing into the red at the chorus as the song's peak

title_hook: The title is past tense and second person, with the narrator as grammatical object: he is defined by the other person's love, and that love is over. This one phrase is what makes the deliberate widening work. 'Loved' is equally true of a partner who left and a grandmother who died, so the same chorus fits both readings Capaldi wanted (SB-S5#P8-P9) without a word changing. Placement: in the press paraphrase the chorus admits to having come to rely on being loved, which suggests the title closes that admission (inferred; not checked against a full lyric). Sound: four short words; anything about where they fall in the bar or how they are sung is text-only, not checked against the recording. Stereogum says the payoff comes from the vocal escalating at the chorus, not from wordplay (SB-S9#paras 16-17).

language_choices.what_it_does: Puts the narrator in the object position and the love in the past, so self-pity becomes self-description. This is the grammatical device that lets one lyric hold a breakup and a bereavement

language_choices.choice: a list of needs: heal / know / hold
language_choices.what_it_does: States need as a run of plain verbs with no object, place or event. Plainness is stronger here because any specific (a flat, a hospital) would settle which loss it is; the cost is that the delivery has to supply the particulars
A worn idiom used to make an admission, not to build an image. It sounds like speech, which keeps the chorus singable and unshowy; Stereogum calls this kind of phrasing greeting-card but deliberate
An idiom listeners complete for themselves. Plugged In read it as implying physical intimacy, which shows how open phrasing invites projection the writers never specified
language_choices.basis: press (SB-S10#'When I Used to Know You' para 3)

language_choices.choice: no concrete images (whole lyric, per critics)
language_choices.what_it_does: Stereogum and the New Statesman describe the lyric as generic, self-pitying and light on images, with the meaning carried by melody and voice. That is the price of the open frame. It is also why the song could carry both an organ-donation charity video and a young-love video without contradiction
language_choices.basis: press (SB-S9#paras 6-7, 16; SB-S11#para 3); videos from SB-S1#Music videos and SB-S15

connective_lines: Only partly visible. In the press paraphrase the song moves by statements of need and admission, not by events; the reviewer describes no scene-setting or time-shift lines (SB-S10). Inference: the in-between lines keep the register level and conversational, so the chorus admission is the only rise and nothing in the verses competes with it. Low confidence, since a full lyric was not legitimately visible.
musical: Documented: Capaldi says the verse melody came from chords the band was playing in a recording session and was saved on his phone, and that he later worked on the chorus and pre-chorus melodies at a piano in his shed (SB-S5#P5-P6). Barnes says Capaldi improvised four chords plus the verse and pre-chorus melodies, then Barnes took the piano and developed the chorus (SB-S8#Emotive Force ¶2); he also told Billboard that Capaldi wrote the melody ten minutes before the session (SB-S7#para 8). These accounts conflict and are left unresolved. Arrangement, from the writers' statements in SOS: essentially one piano (a Keyscape virtual instrument processed to sound less in-the-box, with Adele's 'Someone Like You' as the tonal target); drums proposed and rejected; a string arrangement tried and cut back to the middle eight; light Auto-Tune kept from demo day. Barnes says a simple mix leaves nowhere to hide (SB-S8#Minimalism; Perfectly Imperfect; Nowhere To Hide; Double Exposure). Barnes also mentions three chorus takes and a halftime snare tried and dropped (SB-S7#para 8). Wikipedia lists 110 BPM and D-flat major, uncited (SB-S1). Press: Stereogum describes a raspy vocal pushed into the red at the chorus over a reverb-lush piano (SB-S9#paras 15, 17). Text-only boundary: no melodic, stress or rhythmic claim here was checked against the recording.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lewis Capaldi
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Had the melody finished but parked it, feeling he had said all he wanted about an old relationship; played it to TMS and Romans during a session for an upbeat song; wanted the lyric to be about losing someone in general so others could map their lives onto it; it then came together very quickly.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lewis Capaldi
writer_commentary.paraphrase: About six months overall; the best songs don't come easily. Verse melody from band chords, saved on his phone; chorus and pre-chorus worked on two months later in his garden shed; finished with TMS in about half an hour, stream of consciousness. Kept it open-ended to fit a relationship ending and two family bereavements, having tired of writing about himself.

writer_commentary.speaker: Ben Kohn
writer_commentary.paraphrase: About 90% of the final version came from one three-hour session; it was the second song written that day.

writer_commentary.speaker: Tom Barnes
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The first song that day was bigger and drum-led and stalled after lunch. Capaldi improvised at the piano while an iPad recorded; Barnes took over the piano and developed the chorus; Capaldi offered strong lines that the four of them knitted into a lyric.

writer_commentary.speaker: Pete Kelleher
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The emotion was not discussed as a theme and death was never mentioned; the charity link came later. Verse and chorus on day one, middle eight and second verse a week later.

writer_commentary.speaker: Pete Kelleher and TMS
writer_commentary.paraphrase: They usually overcomplicate and strip back; the small budget was embraced; drums were suggested and rejected; strings clouded the track and were kept minimal and only in the middle eight.

writer_commentary.speaker: Pete Kelleher; Tom Barnes
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Sparse production is unusual for them. Written in about two hours at an August 2018 session; three chorus takes; strings the only element added and then removed; a halftime snare briefly tried. Barnes says Capaldi wrote the melody ten minutes before and wrote the lyric with Kohn and Kelleher. Kelleher says it almost didn't make the album.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Roman
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Met Capaldi about two years before; about a year later they wrote the song at the end of a session, which he calls a Hail Mary moment. No detail on lyric or revisions.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lewis Capaldi (relayed from Daily Star and Billboard)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Repeatedly judged the melodies not good enough and nearly abandoned the song; felt he had written too many heartbreak songs to write another.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lewis Capaldi (relayed from an unnamed Australian channel)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Says the song is about his grandmother, who died a few years earlier, not about an ex.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lewis Capaldi
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Humour is what lets him own his flaws in a relationship honestly; without it the songs would be too closed off.

analyst_inference: The widening was done through grammar, not vagueness: second person, past tense, the narrator as object of the love, and no circumstantial facts. That is why Capaldi's shifting accounts of the subject never contradict the lyric.
Restraint is one decision applied at two scales: plain lyric and one instrument. Each added element was tested against the voice and removed if it competed (drums, most of the strings).

The process accounts conflict on who wrote the chorus melody and how long the session took. The consistent points are that Capaldi brought melody, the lyric was written fast and collaboratively in the room, and a second session added verse two and the middle eight. Nothing documented supports assigning any line to one writer: the TMS accounts describe the lyric room as Capaldi plus TMS, Roman's own account says 'we', and all five share credit (SB-S2).
The critics' charge of 'generic' and the song's reach are the same property seen from two sides: the lyric hands the particulars to the voice.
revisions: No documented before/after lyric lines. Documented changes of scope and arrangement: (1) the subject was widened from one old relationship to loss in general (Capaldi, SB-S3#Q2 and SB-S5#P8-P9; Songfacts credits the push to TMS, SB-S6#fact 7); (2) Capaldi nearly abandoned the melodies more than once before the session (relayed from Daily Star and Billboard, SB-S6#fact 7, SB-S14); (3) the second verse and middle eight were added about a week after day one (SB-S8#Emotive Force ¶3); (4) drums were proposed and rejected, a string arrangement was tried and reduced to the middle eight, and a halftime snare was tried and dropped (SB-S8#Minimalism; SB-S7#para 8).

transferable.craft: To make one ballad fit more than one loss, open it through grammar rather than vagueness: keep 'I' and 'you', put the love in the past tense, keep the narrator's needs and admissions, and leave out only the facts that would say why the other person is gone.
transferable.limits: Critics call the result generic (SB-S9, SB-S11), and it depends on a voice and melody that supply the particulars. A song whose force is a scene (SB-SONG2) would lose its point.

transferable.craft: When the lyric is plain, keep the arrangement as plain as the lyric, and test every addition (drums, strings, a second instrument) by whether it clouds the voice; if a colour stays, give it one section.
transferable.limits: Advice for the room, not the lyric; the app cannot hear whether anything clouds the voice. An up-tempo or band song needs its drums (SB-F14).

transferable.craft: A melody that stalled because its subject repeats your recent songs can be finished by changing the scope of the subject rather than the tune.
transferable.limits: Documented for one song, and accounts differ on whose idea the widening was.

exercise: Synthetic and original, not drawn from the song. Write a two-line chorus to 'you' in the past tense that could be sung about someone who left or someone who died, for example: 'I still lay out two cups at seven / you were the reason mornings had a shape.' Then write a version with one detail that settles it ('since you moved in with him', 'since the funeral'), and note what each version gains and who can no longer sing it.
commercial_note: Kept separate. Capaldi suggested to NME that the plain piano-and-vocal arrangement helped it stand out (relayed, SB-S6#fact 6); Kelleher says it almost didn't make the album (SB-S7#para 9). Charts: seven consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the UK Singles Chart and the UK's best-selling single of 2019; No. 1 on the US Billboard Hot 100 dated 2 November 2019, in its 24th chart week, three non-consecutive weeks at No. 1 (SB-S1#Chart performance); RIAA Diamond (SB-S16). None of this shows why it succeeded.
gaps: No full lyric legitimately visible (licensed sites blocked; no official lyric page; the Vevo Footnotes video was not readable as text). Three Billboard pages (SB-S20 to SB-S22) and an MTV interview (SB-S23) could not be fetched. Process accounts conflict on where the chorus melody came from and how long the session took. No first-person account documents the origin of any particular line. No audio.
builder_note: Sam Roman, who owns this app, is one of the five credited writers. No source here attributes any line to any writer; his own account would outrank every source in this record.

title: Someone Like You
lyric_access: partial: no full lyric seen. Licensed lyric sites are blocked (the same Musixmatch/LyricFind blocks, SB-S18 and SB-S19, so no further providers were tried) and adele.com shows none (SB-S33). What was legitimately visible: Dan Wilson's narrative summary (a woman unexpectedly visits her married ex; the chorus is ironic) (SB-S25); Wikipedia's subject summary citing Adele (SB-S24); Songfacts' editorial notes on one line, the best-for-you line, including the word added in session two (SB-S29); and press identification of melodic moments in the chorus (SB-S24 relaying the Village Voice; SB-S31).
angle: The subject label is an ex who has moved on. In Dan Wilson's account the angle is a brave resolution the narrator doesn't believe: she tells him she'll find someone else, but the title's 'like' gives away that she wants him again (SB-S25#Q5 ¶1). The verse situation is concrete (a visit to a married ex she wasn't invited to make), and Wilson says the writers deliberately made it as personal as possible rather than general (SB-S24#Background, citing Billboard 2011). Adele has framed it as letting go and making peace with the relationship rather than casting him as the villain (relayed, SB-S29).
narrator: First person: a woman addressing the ex inside the scene. Her stance is generous on the surface (she wishes him well) and abject underneath; Adele contrasted it with 'Rolling in the Deep' as the song where she is on her knees (relayed via SB-S24, citing Digital Spy 2011). The ambiguity is that the generosity is sincere and a plea at once. Songfacts says the best-for-you line hands back a phrase the ex had used on her (SB-S29; editorial, no primary quote), so even the kindness has an edge.

section_map.function: Reports the news that he has settled down with someone else. Adele brought the lyrics and melody for at least its first half into the session

Built on a chord series Wilson suggested, then Adele quickly found a line that unlocked the section. Songfacts' editor and a volunteer blog say it runs nine bars instead of eight, like holding a breath before the chorus; no primary Wilson source for that was found
The resolution to find someone like him, which Wilson reads as ironic. Press describes the voice rising an octave on parts of it, and NPR's host locates an appoggiatura on the word 'you'
In Wilson's summary she turns up unexpectedly at the married ex's. At the end of day one this verse had no words (or only part, per PopMatters)
section_map.basis: writer_statement (SB-S25#Q5 ¶1, Q6 ¶2; SB-S26#A3¶2); placing the visit in verse 2 is inferred

section_map.function: Not yet written at the end of day one; its lyric was not legitimately visible
Re-sung on day two because Adele's voice had a rougher edge, which Wilson says gave it more emotion

title_hook: The title is the chorus's resolve, and its meaning turns on one word, 'like'. Said straight, it means moving on; Wilson reads the qualifier as confessing that she wants him again (SB-S25#Q5 ¶1). So the chorus can be sung with full sincerity while meaning the opposite of what it claims. Sound, from press descriptions: NPR's host identifies an appoggiatura on 'you' in the chorus (SB-S31), and the Village Voice describes an octave rise on parts of the chorus (via SB-S24). Placement within the chorus and the number of repetitions were not verified against a full lyric.

language_choices.what_it_does: Turns a resilient claim into an admission without changing its tone; the irony needs no wink

language_choices.choice: a concrete situation: married ex, uninvited visit
language_choices.what_it_does: Gives the verses checkable facts instead of mood, and plain report of what happened makes the chorus feeling credible. Wilson says the aim was maximum personal detail, not lyrics general enough for anyone
Songfacts says it repeats a phrase the ex used on her, and that Adele added 'too' in the second session. If so, the one added word turns his consolation into her reply
language_choices.basis: press (SB-S29; editorial, no primary quote); the 'reply' reading is inference

language_choices.what_it_does: Wilson names keeping it simple, direct and personal as his main contribution, and says he mostly stayed out of the words, which carried Adele's story

connective_lines: Only partly visible. Wilson's description implies the verses carry report (the news, the visit) so that the chorus can be pure resolve. He also says the pre-chorus line Adele found quickly is what let the rest of that section fall into place (SB-S25#Q3 ¶4): one strong line can make the joins around it easy. Low confidence, since a full lyric was not legitimately visible.
musical: Documented: Adele began the verse on guitar and switched to piano when Wilson played it, saying the piano was more inspiring (SB-S25#Q3 ¶2). Wilson tried to make the piano part feel like a performance so she would want to sing to it (SB-S26#A3¶2), and the Star Tribune's narration says he embellished her melody with large classical chords (SB-S30). He recorded the demo with high-quality microphones and signal chain on purpose so it could stand as a final record, and an orchestral version was not better than the demo (SB-S28#Q&A 1-2). Wikipedia lists A major, 67.5 BPM, three chord progressions, a vocal range of F#3 to E5, and voice plus a looping piano line (SB-S24#Composition; not independently checked). Press: the Village Voice on the octave rise in the chorus (via SB-S24); NPR's host on the appoggiatura on 'you', with John Sloboda describing such ornaments as small tensions resolved by the next chord (SB-S31). Songfacts' editor says the higher second half of the chorus was Wilson's idea and that Adele found it uncomfortable (SB-S29; no primary source found). The SOS piece on SB-SONG1 says TMS used this song's piano as their tonal target (SB-S8). Text-only boundary: nothing here was checked against the recording.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Adele came in with lyrics and melody for at least the first half of the verse and wanted to write about her heartbreak; he thinks his main contribution was helping keep the song simple, direct and personal.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: She switched him from guitar to piano. There were no arguments: she knew what she wanted to say, and he mostly did the music and chord changes and stayed out of the words. He suggested a pre-chorus chord series and she quickly found the line. On day two he had her re-sing the final chorus.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: A love song from the perspective of a woman who unexpectedly visits her married ex; the chorus is ironic, since she says she'll find someone else but wants someone like him.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Meant as a demo, with strings and choir expected later. At the end of day one it was affecting but only half-written, with no words for the second verse or bridge. Her manager loved it and her mother cried; the demo stayed on the album.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Chose the sadder of two starts; two days of work; the rough mix lacked the bridge and part of verse two and had different choruses; made the piano a performance to inspire her; recorded the demo at high fidelity to impress Rick Rubin.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Adele had the lyrical story and he supported it musically as strongly as he could; as a lyricist he offered word suggestions and tested whether new lines survived.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Had demo-itis about his version and never expected it to be released; an orchestral version was nice but not better; after earlier experiences he records demos well enough to stand as finals.

writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Rejects the idea of appoggiaturas as a secret trick; a good song lets listeners retrace what the writers felt, and he and Adele imaginatively reconstructed what she was really going through.

writer_commentary.source: SB-S30#'If you're going to write a song'
writer_commentary.speaker: Dan Wilson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: A song needs the writer to be vulnerable and to draw on real feelings and events.

writer_commentary.source: SB-S24#Background (relaying Digital Spy 2011 and a 2010 radio interview)
writer_commentary.speaker: Adele
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Imagined finding him content with a family at around 40 while she was alone, which frightened her; contrasted the song with 'Rolling in the Deep' as the one where she is on her knees; they wrote it on piano and recorded it as soon as it was written.

writer_commentary.source: SB-S29#meaning facts (relaying Q, MTV News, The Sun)
writer_commentary.speaker: Adele
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Wrote the start at the end of her bed; writing it let her make peace with the relationship rather than portray him as the villain; called it simply letting go.

analyst_inference: The frame was narrowed on purpose (a real situation, a married ex) and the song still travelled. Beside SB-SONG1, this shows that open and personal frames both work, and that the choice decides which lines can be plain: here the verses are plain report and the chorus is plain resolve.
The irony sits in one qualifier, so no line has to signal it; that is why the song can be sung straight.
Restraint here was partly circumstance (a demo made under deadline became the record), as the budget was for SB-SONG1. In both cases the writers then defended the sparse version against a fuller one.

Division of labour, in Wilson's account: the artist's story and words, the co-writer's music and simplicity. In a ballad session, Songroom could treat the co-writer's job as protecting the artist's plain words rather than adding lines.
revisions: Documented: at the end of day one the song was about two-thirds written, with no words for the second verse or bridge and choruses that differed from the final (SB-S26#A3¶1-2; SB-S25#Q6 ¶2). The final chorus was re-sung on day two for a rougher, more emotional voice (SB-S25#Q3 ¶6). Wilson once suggested a line change but does not say which (SB-S25#Q3). An orchestral version was made and judged no better than the demo, which became the record (SB-S28#Q&A 1). Songfacts' editorial, with no primary quote, says Adele added 'too' to the best-for-you line in the second session and that her other song start became 'Rumour Has It' (SB-S29). No before/after line text is documented.

transferable.craft: Let one small qualifier in a resilient chorus claim ('like', 'almost', 'still') admit the opposite of the claim, and let the verses make the real wish clear, so the chorus can be sung with full sincerity.
transferable.limits: If the verses don't establish the real wish, listeners hear only the brave surface. The irony reading is the co-writer's, not something tested on listeners.

transferable.craft: In a personal ballad, put the checkable facts of the situation in the verses as plain report and keep the chorus to one resolve; don't widen the facts to make it 'relatable'.
transferable.limits: Close to C43 (specific verses, universal chorus); the distinct point is that the writers refused to generalise at all. A song meant to fit many losses (SB-SONG1) needs the opposite.

transferable.craft: In a ballad session, the co-writer's job can be to keep the artist's words simple and direct, and to make the accompaniment something the singer wants to sing to, rather than to add lines.
transferable.limits: Depends on an artist who arrives knowing what they want to say; facing a blank page, the co-writer has to bring words.

exercise: Synthetic and original, not a rewrite of any line in the song. Take a resilient claim such as 'I'm doing better now' and write three versions, each adding one qualifier ('mostly', 'some days', 'on paper'). For each, write one verse fact that makes the qualifier's confession unmistakable, and keep the claim itself calm.
commercial_note: Kept separate. It reached UK No. 1 after Adele's BRIT Awards performance in February 2011 and was the UK's biggest-selling single of 2011; it spent five weeks at No. 1 on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 2011 (SB-S24#Chart performance). Wilson says listeners who don't know Adele told him it made them cry (SB-S25#Q6), and explains the response as listeners retracing the writers' feelings (SB-S31). None of this shows why it succeeded.
gaps: No full lyric legitimately visible. Adele's own words reach this file only through Wikipedia and Songfacts relays (Digital Spy, Q, MTV News and The Sun were not fetched). The 2011 Billboard cover story was not fetched and the WSJ piece was blocked. The nine-bar pre-chorus, the higher chorus register being Wilson's idea, and the added 'too' rest on Songfacts editorial or a volunteer blog with no primary quote. No audio.

title: Girl Crush
lyric_access: partial: no official or licensed full display was reachable. Little Big Town's site has no lyrics (SC-S13), and Musixmatch (SC-S11) and LyricFind (SC-S12) are blocked. Seen: the fetch tool's structural description of the lyric block on Wide Open Country's editorial page (SC-S5): stanzas, line counts, title positions and what each stanza does. No licence notice was visible there, so the licence is unverified. Also seen: short fragments quoted in Plugged In's review (SC-S6; not stored), press paraphrase (SC-S2, SC-S3, CT-S88) and the writers' accounts of the opening (SC-S1, CT-S36, CT-S37). I did not see the lyric text itself and stored none.
angle: Topic: jealousy of the woman a man has chosen over the narrator. Angle: the jealousy is told as a crush on the rival, an inventory of her body that the narrator wants because the man is close to it. The everyday phrase for admiring another woman is not reversed but pushed to a covetous extreme. Nobody is attacked; the narrator's want is the whole song.
narrator: A woman (sung by Karen Fairchild) speaks to the man as 'you' from the chorus onward, and about the rival in the third person: a three-way I / you / her. Her stance, per the press and tool descriptions, is reluctant admission and consuming longing, not blame. Two ambiguities remain. Is the man an ex who left for the rival (Fairchild, SC-S2; Schlapman via SC-S3; Plugged In, SC-S6), or someone she never had (CMT's reading via CT-S88)? The descriptions suggest the text doesn't settle it. And is the desire, on first hearing, for the woman? The writers say they never imagined that reading (SC-S1); some radio listeners heard it (SC-S3).

section_map.function: Opens with the title in its first line, framed as an admission of an attraction the narrator can't control. On its own it reads as desire for the other woman, and the man is not yet addressed. Lindsey sang the opening lines first, before anyone discussed what the title meant.
section_map.basis_note: structure and line count from the fetch tool's description of the SC-S5 lyric block (text not seen; licence not shown); order of writing from SC-S1 para 5, CT-S36 para 4, CT-S37

section_map.function: Lists what she covets of the rival (lips, perfume, hair, touch, per SC-S5 para 2) and addresses the man as 'you' for the first time. It supplies the reason: she wants to be the rival so he would want her. Ends on the title, and this is where the meaning settles.
section_map.basis_note: SC-S5 lyric block as described by the tool; SC-S6 reads the real desire as winning back the ex

section_map.function: Sleeplessness and obsessive imagining of the couple together. It adds no new reason and no new detail of the rival; it keeps the want present and physical until the chorus returns.
The first four lines repeat; the last line changes and returns to the title idea.
Repeats the opening admission with one word changed, so the song ends where it began; by now the listener knows what the title means.
section_map.basis_note: SC-S5 tool description; 'now the listener knows' is my inference

section_map.function: No bridge appears in the described block. McKenna's remark that listeners should hear a whole song, not just a chorus (SC-S1 para 11), suits a form in which the opening is only understood after the chorus.

title_hook: Placement: the title is the first thing sung and closes each chorus. The described block has five occurrences: the first line of verse 1, twice in the chorus's last line, the changed last line of chorus 2, and the first line of the coda. Nothing about the phrase itself is held back; what is held back is its reason, which arrives in the chorus. Delayed meaning: the everyday sense (admiring a woman, wanting to be like her; SC-S1, CT-S36) is half true, and the chorus redirects it to the man. Payoff: an explanation, not a trick; the writers' worry was whether the jealousy would be understood (SC-S1 para 8). Sound: text-only. No writer or press statement about how the title is sung was found.

language_choices.choice: the title phrase itself (a social-media hashtag)
language_choices.what_it_does: Brings in a phrase listeners use for harmless admiration, so its sensual use is a surprise. Because 'wanting to be her' is already part of its everyday sense, the jealousy reading needs no twisting of the words.
language_choices.basis_note: origin from SC-S1 and CT-S36; the 'already part of its sense' point is my inference

language_choices.choice: the opening framed as an admission
language_choices.what_it_does: The narrator offers the title as something she is reluctant to confess. That makes the listener lean in, and it also invites the misreading. Plain statement, no imagery.
language_choices.basis_note: SC-S5 tool description; SC-S6 calls it an opening confession

language_choices.choice: the rival's body as an inventory (lips, perfume, hair, touch)
language_choices.what_it_does: Concrete, sensory nouns that belong to the other woman carry the jealousy. Each is something the man is close to, so the list is about him while seeming to be about her. Fairchild says this sensual writing puts some listeners off at first until the hook changes their view (SC-S2).
language_choices.basis_note: nouns as listed in SC-S5 para 2 (press paraphrase); their function is my inference

language_choices.what_it_does: A plain causal line, the first to address the man, redirects the whole list. Plainness matters here: a clever reason would pull attention away from the turn.
language_choices.basis_note: SC-S5 tool description; the point about plainness is my inference

language_choices.what_it_does: An ordinary physical symptom of obsession stops the second verse repeating the inventory and grounds the want in real nights, not only fantasy.

connective_lines: Visible only as described. Verse 2 does connective work: a plain report of sleeplessness and of picturing the couple, with no new reason and no new detail of the rival, so the chorus's reason lands again instead of competing with a second idea. The coda changes a single word of the opening, which marks a return rather than a new statement. Not every line is a punchline: the inventory carries the images, the reason line carries the turn, and the rest reports a state (text-only, from the tool's description).
musical: Writer statements: Lindsey wrote the opening by ear on guitar, mostly with barre chords, in 6/8, using a progression McKenna calls slightly unusual (SC-S1 paras 5-6). The writers call it sparse, sexy and sultry, an open canvas; McKenna praises the restraint of the band and producer Jay Joyce, and says Fairchild sang the lead with people in the room (CT-S36 para 7; SC-S1). Publisher sheet listing (SC-S7, an SSA choir arrangement): 6/8, C major, 'moderately slow'. Wikipedia, citing a Musicnotes listing (CT-S88): about 58 dotted-quarter beats per minute, C–Em–F–G, lead range G3–A4. That printed pattern does not look unusual, so McKenna's description is unresolved. Press: stripped-down production on a walking, blues-inspired guitar line (SC-S4); 'sparse' and 'haunting' (SC-S5 para 3). Text-only boundary: no melodic, stress or delivery claim of mine; nothing was checked by listening.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lori McKenna
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The title came from her phone list; she knew it as a hashtag for admiration but not what it meant as a song. Rose suggested moving on. Lindsey sang the opening lines by ear without asking what the title meant, in 6/8 with barre chords and an odd progression. Rose's notebook drove it to the end, and it was finished within the hour.
writer_commentary.quote: the song was really in charge that morning

writer_commentary.speaker: Lori McKenna
writer_commentary.paraphrase: They sent the voice memo to publisher Scott Rose asking only whether it made sense. Their doubt was whether a woman wanting a man who is with another woman would be understood; they never imagined it heard as a woman wanting a woman.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lori McKenna
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Listeners should hear a whole song, not only a chorus; she cites 'He Stopped Loving Her Today'.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lori McKenna
writer_commentary.paraphrase: No demo was made; the phone memo, possibly sung from wrong lyrics, is what the band asked to keep. She praises the band's restraint.

writer_commentary.speaker: Lori McKenna; Hillary Lindsey
writer_commentary.paraphrase: They never discussed the title, and it could have been an empowerment song. Lindsey wrote the first verse on Rose's Gibson and sang the first four lines, which fixed what the song would be. Written in about an hour and a half and recorded on a phone; no demo.

writer_commentary.speaker: Hillary Lindsey
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Title first, and nobody knew what to do with it. The first verse came almost at once and set the direction; the writers offered lines in turn; about 40 minutes.

writer_commentary.speaker: Liz Rose; Hillary Lindsey (via a Rolling Stone recap of Broken Record)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Rose turned the idea down at first and agreed once Lindsey began playing what became the opening line. Lindsey says she wasn't consciously thinking.

writer_commentary.speaker: Karen Fairchild (performer, not a writer)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: A woman speaking to her ex about why he loves someone else. The sensual writing may put some off at first, but the hook changes their view. Rose pitched it saying the band would never cut it.

analyst_inference: The turn is an explanation: the chorus doesn't contradict the opening's desire, it gives the reason for it, so a first hearing is not a cheat.

The phrase's everyday sense includes wanting to be like the woman; the song pushes that to covetousness rather than reversing it. That is why the title can hold both readings for the length of verse 1.

Because the reason lives in the chorus, a listener who hears only the opening and the bodily inventory can come away with the reading the writers never imagined (SC-S1). This is the craft side of the 2015 radio episode (SC-S3).
The quick, undiscussed start (title, then Lindsey's sung opening) meant the first sung lines chose the angle rather than a debate did (consistent with CT-F15).
revisions: None documented. McKenna describes no changes during the writing (SC-S1). Lindsey wanted to re-sing the phone memo, but Fairchild and Schlapman asked to keep it. McKenna says the memo may have been sung from wrong lyrics, but what differed is not documented. Session length differs between tellings: about 40 minutes (CT-S37), within the hour (SC-S1), about an hour and a half (CT-S36).

transferable.craft: Turn a phrase by pushing its everyday sense to an extreme rather than reversing it; then the first reading is partly true and the turn feels earned.
transferable.limits: Needs a phrase whose ordinary meaning already holds the seed (admiring her, wanting to be her). With a phrase that has only one sense, this becomes a straight idiom flip (C29).

transferable.craft: Explanation payoff: state the misleadable title in line one, put the reason (addressed to the real object of the feeling) in the chorus, and keep the reason line plain.
transferable.limits: Fails where listeners stop early (radio skims, clips). Genre limit: the misreading it turns against was the default assumption of a 2015 country-radio audience; for another audience, or a queer artist, the same-sex reading may be the point, not the risk.

transferable.craft: Envy as inventory: carry jealousy through concrete things that belong to the rival, each chosen because the addressee is close to it.
transferable.limits: If the reason never arrives, a list of looks reads as petty or objectifying; a list of generic beauty nouns is just props (compare C11).

transferable.craft: Check a turn's clarity with one outside listener and one question (does it make sense?) before polishing.
transferable.limits: An insider confirms clarity, not reception; Scott Rose's yes did not predict the radio reading.

exercise: Synthetic, not a rewrite. Take an online phrase of admiration used about someone else, such as 'goals'. Write a four-line opening in which the narrator admits, plainly, that she calls her parents' old wedding photos 'goals'. Then write a chorus whose second-to-last line gives the reason, addressed to one parent: the photos are the only place the two of them still stand together. Test: read only the opening to someone and ask what the song is about, then read the chorus. If their answer changes and the second answer still contains the first, the turn works; if the first answer was simply wrong, the opening is a trick.
commercial_note: Kept separate. US Hot Country Songs No. 1 for 13 weeks; Country Airplay peak No. 3; Hot 100 peak No. 18 (week ending 2015-05-09) (CT-S88, SC-S3). Billboard reportedly found it played on 139 of 145 reporting country stations despite the publicised complaints (relayed by SC-S3); American Songwriter's view that airplay would otherwise have gone higher is speculation. It won two Grammys, including Best Country Song (CT-S88). None of this explains why it succeeded.

The Musicnotes data comes from an SSA arrangement and from a listing cited by Wikipedia, and McKenna's 'unusual progression' remains unexplained. No audio.

title: Something in the Orange
lyric_access: partial: no official or licensed full display was reachable. zachbryan.com has no lyrics (SC-S22), and the Musixmatch and LyricFind domains are blocked (SC-S11, SC-S12). Seen: the fetch tool's stanza-by-stanza description of the full lyric block on Holler's editorial lyrics-and-meaning page (SC-S14): line counts, addressee, light sources, tense and title positions. The footer shows only Holler's own copyright, with no lyric licence, so the licence is unverified. Also seen: short phrases of four words or fewer cited in Robin Frederick's song guide (SC-S15; not stored). I did not see the lyric text itself and stored none.
angle: Topic: a relationship ending. Angle: a man who can't decide what's true lets the colour of the light decide for him, and it tells him two opposite things: first that they're not done, then that she isn't coming back. In the end he stops reading the light and asks her outright to turn around. The song is about wanting a sign as much as about the breakup.
narrator: A man speaks to 'you' in every stanza (per the tool's description), and the lover never answers. His stance moves through reassurance, doubt, devotion that isn't returned and self-punishment (drinking, per the tool), and ends on a direct plea. Two ambiguities are unresolved and text-only. Is the orange a sunset or a sunrise? Bryan's first account says sunset; Frederick reads verse 1 as sunrise; the tool reads dusk, then morning sun. And has she already gone at the end? Frederick says she has and he pleads; the tool reads it as conditional.

section_map.function: Reassurance to 'you' in the orange light (dusk per the tool, sunrise per Frederick); hopeful; no title.
He senses she doesn't feel the same but isn't ready to let go; morning light. Ends on the first title line, completed with hope that they're not finished.
section_map.basis_note: SC-S14 tool description; SC-S15 cites a short line to this effect

section_map.function: Devotion that isn't returned, drinking as self-punishment and a rhetorical question. Ends on the title completed with the opposite verdict: she isn't coming back. Frederick calls it loss and frustration and says the chorus speeds up its words and notes.
Memory and a plea to be taken back. The orange is now the glow of an artificial bulb seen in her eyes, which Holler's commentary reads as false affection.
