title_hook: Placement: absent from verse 1, first heard as the last line of verse 2, then as the last line of each chorus (four times in the Holler block), and absent from the final stanza. Form: an unfinished frame, in which a vague 'something' in a colour 'tells' him a verdict; the completion changes from hope (verse 2) to loss (chorus). Delayed meaning: the colour is never explained, only moved to different lights. Image against charge: orange usually suggests sunshine and energy, which cuts against loss (SC-S15). Payoff: the same frame line delivering the opposite verdict, then a last stanza that abandons the frame for a direct plea. Sound: text-only. No writer or press statement about how the title is sung; Frederick says the chorus speeds up its words and notes (analyst).

language_choices.choice: 'something' plus a colour as the title
language_choices.what_it_does: A vague pronoun and a single colour word: the narrator can't name what he sees, so the title admits uncertainty. Plainness is the point, and the one concrete word is a colour, not a story. On Bryan's first account he fixed on the word itself (SC-S16, CW-S49).
language_choices.basis_note: origin relayed by press; the function is my inference

language_choices.choice: the frame verb: the light 'tells' him
language_choices.what_it_does: Hands his judgement to the light. He reads signs instead of asking, and that is what the ending reverses.
language_choices.basis_note: SC-S14 tool description; the interpretation is mine

language_choices.choice: the colour moved: evening and morning sun, a bulb in her eyes, headlights, light on everything
language_choices.what_it_does: One image carried across natural and artificial light tracks what he believes. Frederick says the colour is clarified in three places, from hope to a harsh bulb to loss and anger.
language_choices.basis_note: SC-S14 tool description; SC-S15 (analyst); the two disagree on which verse holds which light

language_choices.choice: a few loaded single words in plain syntax (Frederick lists six, e.g. 'poison', 'damned')
language_choices.what_it_does: Frederick says a handful of emotionally loaded words carry darkness and fear that a plain statement of fear would not; the syntax around them stays conversational.

language_choices.choice: lines of four words or fewer
language_choices.what_it_does: Frederick cites a brief line about missing her and one about not being finished. Short, flat statements carry the hope and the need without decoration.

language_choices.choice: drinking as self-punishment in the chorus
language_choices.what_it_does: A stock country/Americana gesture, stated plainly, that marks resignation. It is genre-coded rather than original.

connective_lines: As described, the verses carry the situation in plain statements (reassurance, doubt, memory) while the light images carry the change. In the chorus, the rhetorical question and the drinking line are plain connecting statements between the devotion line and the title's verdict. The final stanza's repeated closing line is a plea, not an image. Not every line is a punchline: the title line is the only one built to land (text-only, from the tool's description and Frederick).
musical: Writer: no statement on the music. Producer Ryan Hadlock (CW-S48, Variety via AOL): Bryan played it on a couch, vocal and guitar were tracked together live in the open room, then lap steel, upright bass and light drums were added; finished in a day. Hadlock (SC-S20): the aim was real-feeling, personal and intimate. Press: a second version, 'Z&E's Version', was produced by Eddie Spear (SC-S18, SC-S19). Descriptions of each version's instruments conflict: strings and piano on Hadlock's (SC-S18); acoustic guitar and harmonica on Z&E's (SC-S19, citing Rolling Stone); lap steel, upright bass and drums (CW-S48). Analyst (SC-S15, Robin Frederick): no pre-chorus or bridge; the verse melody rocks, lines 1 and 3 rising slightly and 2 and 4 falling; the chorus speeds up its words and notes with a new rhythm; verse Em7–D–G and G–D–Em7, chorus C–G–D then Em; acoustic and rough-edged; vocal believability over pitch. Text-only boundary: none of this was checked by listening, and Frederick's notes are her own transcription.

writer_commentary.speaker: Zach Bryan (relayed)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Not about a breakup or anything dark: in a Wisconsin cabin watching a sunset, he fixed on the word 'orange' and thought it would make a good story for a song.
writer_commentary.quote: that's a cool story to tell in a song

writer_commentary.speaker: Zach Bryan (relayed from Apple Music, Today's Country Radio with Kelleigh Bannen)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The same cabin-and-sunset account; people assume it is about something deep and dark.

writer_commentary.speaker: Zach Bryan (relayed from fan footage of a 2024 Quittin' Time tour show)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: He wrote it after being stood up on a date, and that was the whole story.

writer_commentary.speaker: Ryan Hadlock (producer)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Bryan had written it in the cabin before the session. He played it on a couch, it was tracked live and finished in a day, and Bryan was in tears at the end.

analyst_inference: The title is a frame, not a statement: the words stay fixed while the verdict changes, so the turn needs no new vocabulary.
The narrator reads signs instead of asking. The final plea, which drops the title, is the one moment he acts, a change of stance that does a bridge's job in a form without a bridge.
Bryan's two origin stories conflict, and neither describes the lyric's breakup. The meaning is carried by the text, not the anecdote, so the anecdote is no guide to rewriting the song.
Plain syntax, a few loaded single words and one colour amount to restraint: the song spends its imagery on a single object.
revisions: None documented. The two released versions (Hadlock's single and Eddie Spear's 'Z&E's Version') differ in production; no lyric changes are documented. Bryan posted snippets on social media in December 2021 (SC-S19); whether they differ from the release is not documented.

transferable.craft: A frame title with a changing verdict: write the title as an unfinished clause the narrator reads ('X tells me ___') and complete it differently each time, hopefully at the end of a verse and finally in the chorus.
transferable.limits: The hopeful completion has to be heard; if verse 2's title line is cut or buried, the chorus is just a sad line. A frame with nothing concrete to read ('something tells me') is a cliché.

transferable.craft: Move a recurring image: give it a new source each time it returns (natural light, artificial light, a departure), and make each move coincide with a change in belief.
transferable.limits: Frederick's warning: if listeners miss the shifts, the title reads as vague. In a dense or fast lyric the shifts may not register.

transferable.craft: End a song without a bridge by dropping the title and switching from interpreting to asking outright.
transferable.limits: If the plea only restates the chorus feeling, the tag adds length, not change.

transferable.craft: Spend the imagery on one object; keep the syntax plain and let a few loaded single words carry the darkness.
transferable.limits: Genre limit: the rough take, plain syntax, drinking and headlights are Americana/country marks of authenticity. In a polished pop production the same plainness may read as unfinished, and the stock images as borrowed.

exercise: Synthetic, not a rewrite. Pick a sound the narrator keeps hearing, such as the radio left on in the kitchen. Write the frame line 'the radio in the kitchen keeps saying ___' and give it two completions: one that hopes (she's only out late) and one that concludes (she took the good coat). Put the hopeful one as the last line of verse 2 and the conclusion as the last line of the chorus. Then move the sound three times (the kitchen radio, a car radio idling outside, silence when the batteries die) and tie each move to a change in what he believes. Finish with a stanza that drops the frame and asks her one direct thing.
commercial_note: Kept separate. Hot 100 debut on the chart dated 2022-05-07, peak No. 10, his first Hot 100 entry. No. 1 on Hot Country Songs and on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs (week not given); No. 13 on the 2023 year-end Hot 100 (SC-S19). It reached No. 10 without being sent to country radio (CW-S48). Frederick suspects film and TV placements helped (SC-S15, speculation). None of this explains why it succeeded.
gaps: No licensed or official lyric display was reachable. The text features rest on a tool's description of Holler's lyric block (licence unverified) and on short phrases in an analyst's guide. The two descriptions disagree on the number of choruses, on sunrise versus dusk in verse 1, and on whether she has gone by the end. Every Bryan statement is relayed (an Apple Music interview, a deleted post, fan footage); no first-person transcript was found, and Whiskey Riff's December 2024 piece failed to load (SC-S21). There is no writer commentary on any line. No audio; the melodic and chord notes are an analyst's transcription.
lyric_basis_note: Lyric seen only as the fetch tool's description of a press page that prints it (licence not shown); no lyric is stored here.

title: Stick Season
lyric_access: partial: sung excerpts printed in the Song Exploder 247 transcript (ST-S1, re-read 2026-10-19 by tool extract): the verse as first posted (about 10 lines), the chorus as posted on 29 October (about 9 lines), two sketches from the morning of 29 October, two lines of the second verse, chorus fragments, and the outro (about 3 lines). Most of the second verse was not seen. The excerpts run in the order of the writing story, so the section order is inferred. No official or licensed lyric page was found; uDiscover (SS-S9) shows only the final line. Unlicensed lyric sites in search results were not opened.
angle: The subject label is a break-up in a Vermont autumn. The angle is a man left behind in his hometown in the dead season who says out loud that half of it is his fault and then performs his self-pity anyway, so the confession and the sulk arrive together. The season is the relationship's in-between state (colour gone, no snow yet), and Kahan says he meant the picture to be hopeful because the season ends (SS-S9).
narrator: First person, close to Kahan himself: he says the friends-coming-home line and the second verse come straight from his life (ST-S1). The verse speaks to the departed partner as 'you'; the chorus reaches her sideways, through her mother having forgotten him; the second verse drops the partner and turns to his father's depression and his own, with no addressee. The stance is self-mocking self-pity. One meaningful ambiguity: the dream line concedes he may never really have had the person, which makes the loss partly imagined and softens the blame the verse hands out.

section_map.function: Sets up the driving metaphor: a promise made, a change of heart halfway through the drive, the other person passing his exit and keeping going. Then status lines (anger against self-blame, the weather reminding him, a doctor's advice to travel blocked by the pandemic) and a crude closing couplet that pushes blame back at her.

Names the state and the season; reports her mother forgetting he exists; admits half the fault, then claims the victim role; announces drinking alone until his friends are home for Christmas; dreams nightly of a version of her; concedes he never had what he lost.

Turns from the partner to the family: trying to stack good things on top of bad ones, and darkness inherited from his father. Kahan says it took days over Thanksgiving and he kept it because the discomfort might help someone. Only two lines seen.

section_map.section: lift after verse 2 and final chorus
section_map.function: Lift from harmonies that lock to the melody rather than from new words. A gang-vocal last chorus was tried, meant to sound like his friends were home; management thought it might be corny and it was reworked.
Takes stock of what she left (tyre tracks, one pair of shoes) and accepts being split in two as enough. Kahan says the last line is about acknowledging an ending and accepting what comes (SS-S9).

title_hook: The title is a regional term most listeners won't know. Kahan chose it because it is regional and because the bare stretch between autumn and winter works as a metaphor for change in a relationship (SS-S8 Q8). It is not in the posted verse; it arrives in the chorus's opening lines in an inverted form, 'season of the sticks', which he had used for an earlier unreleased interlude (ST-S1 opening). In the excerpts seen it is sung once per chorus, not hammered. The payoff: the season explains why he is stuck (no one is around until Christmas) and promises that it will pass. Sound: text-only, not checked against the recording.

language_choices.choice: the driving metaphor (exit passed, kept going)
language_choices.what_it_does: An everyday physical event carries the whole break-up without naming a feeling. Kahan says he chose driving to show someone who wants to leave, or be left, but can't.

The narrator names his own bad habit before the listener can, so the self-pity is forgivable because it is confessed. The morning sketch had a clinical label ('narcissistic') in the same slot; the posted chorus swaps it for a behaviour.
A small, checkable social humiliation stands in for the larger rejection; the ex is reached through someone else.

Plain, specific and slightly funny. Kahan calls it one of his favourite lines and says it is literal (counting down to 20 December, when college friends came home to Strafford). Its strength is plainness: no image, just a plan.

Date-stamps the song, which risks ageing it; Kahan says it landed with crowds on the first post-pandemic tour. It appears in both the posted verse and the posted chorus excerpts, and whether it moved or repeats is unclear.

language_choices.choice: tyre tracks and one pair of shoes
language_choices.what_it_does: Ends on residue rather than a feeling word: what is physically left after she drove on.

connective_lines: In the verse, the lines between the driving image and the closing couplet are status reports (anger against the truth, the weather reminding him, the blocked trip). They carry mood and time without adding a second metaphor. In the chorus, local facts (the state, the mother, Christmas) alternate with admissions (half the fault, the victim, the drinking), so no line has to be a punchline; the admissions do the connecting. Text-only and partial: most of verse 2 was not seen.
musical: Writer statements only (ST-S1): the chorus reuses the verse's chord progression because he felt a folk song should stay simple. He found the chorus by singing in a borrowed country twang and trying falsetto. Producer Gabe Simon used the guitar's pick guard as a kick-drum-like rhythm and played banjo. The first take was guitar and vocal to a click, and Kahan wanted to keep the casual, not self-serious energy of the phone demo. Harmonies come after verse 2 and in the final chorus; gang vocals were drafted then reworked. Text-only boundary: no claim about melody, stress, or where the title falls in the bar.

writer_commentary.speaker: Noah Kahan
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The song is about being stuck at home, wanting to leave or be left but unable to, with a sense that some of the blame is his; he set it to the metaphor of driving.

writer_commentary.speaker: Noah Kahan
writer_commentary.paraphrase: He wrote the chorus on the morning of 29 October over the verse chords, loosened up by singing in a twang, because the posted verse had drawn hundreds of comments asking for the rest.

writer_commentary.speaker: Noah Kahan
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The second verse, about his father's depression and his own, took several days over Thanksgiving in Vermont; he hoped being open might help listeners as other artists had helped him.

writer_commentary.speaker: Noah Kahan
writer_commentary.paraphrase: Management said the big gang vocal might be corny for such an intimate song; he agreed, re-recorded at length, and thinks a more nuanced approach would have been better.

writer_commentary.speaker: Noah Kahan (release statement)
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The foliage turning grey before the snow is his image for familiar lovers becoming heartbroken strangers; he wants the song heard as hopeful, and the last line is about acknowledging the ending and accepting the future.

writer_commentary.speaker: Noah Kahan
writer_commentary.paraphrase: He wrote it late at night on the way back from a session for his second album, as a folkier escape from a pop-leaning track, and chose the regional term deliberately as a metaphor for change that looks ugly before it resolves.

analyst_inference: The chorus carries the most local material (the state, her mother, the Christmas homecoming) while the verse carries the portable image (a drive). That reverses the common split in which verses are private and the chorus general (card C43). Each local fact in the chorus sits beside an admission anyone could make, which may be why the specificity Kahan feared would alienate people did not.
The song defuses self-pity by letting the narrator name it. A listener does not have to judge a narrator who has already judged himself, and the joke keeps the confession from sounding like a plea.

The heaviest material (inherited depression) arrives only in verse 2, after the hook is established. That came from the order he wrote and posted the parts, but it also works as structure: a break-up song that deepens into a family one.
The dream line, which concedes he may never have had the person, makes the loss partly imaginary. It quietly withdraws the verse's blame and prepares the accepting outro.
revisions: (1) Visible in ST-S1 but not commented on by Kahan: the morning sketch of the chorus used a clinical self-label ('narcissistic') where the posted chorus has 'play the victim', and a sketch line about sensing her gaze became the concession that he may never have had her. The sketch was half-improvised, so treat this as the direction of change, not a draft history. (2) Writer statement: a gang-vocal last chorus was recorded with Gabe Simon and engineer Konrad Snyder, flagged by management as possibly corny, and reworked over a long period with more weight on harmonies; how much of the gang vocal survived is not stated. (3) The title phrase came from an earlier, unreleased interlude. No full earlier lyric is documented.

transferable.craft: A chorus can hold the most local detail if every local fact is paired with an admission anyone could make; move the portable image into the verse.
transferable.limits: A chorus of local facts with no plain admission becomes a postcard. It also needs a voice that already sounds like it is from there.

transferable.craft: Have the narrator name his own bad behaviour (an action, like playing the victim) instead of using a self-diagnosis word; the listener forgives what has already been admitted.
transferable.limits: Repeated every few lines, the self-aware wink becomes a shield and the song reads as evasive.

transferable.craft: Keep the verse chords for the chorus and change the chorus's stance through the voice (a borrowed accent or register) rather than new harmony.
transferable.limits: A writer statement about one folk song. In a form that depends on a harmonic lift, the same chords can flatten the chorus unless melody or register clearly moves.

transferable.craft: Give the last chorus's wish to texture (harmony) rather than acting it out literally (a crowd singing the homecoming).
transferable.limits: Kahan's and his management's judgement on an intimate song; in a deliberate anthem, literal staging can be the point.

exercise: Synthetic, not a rewrite: set a song in an invented seaside town in February. Write a four-line chorus in which every line pairs one local fact (a named closed cafe, the last ferry time) with one admission anyone could make. Then write the same chorus with the local facts removed, and ask which version a stranger would believe.
commercial_note: Kahan's own account: the posted verse drew hundreds of comments overnight, and the song was built in public on TikTok (ST-S1); he was surprised that something so specific to his life connected (ST-S3). Chart peaks per ST-S4, weeks not given: UK Official Singles Chart No. 1, US Billboard Hot 100 No. 9. No causal claim is made here.
gaps: Most of verse 2 not seen. Section order inferred from transcript excerpts that run in writing order. Whether the pandemic line sits in the verse, the chorus or both is ambiguous. Kahan never discusses the mother line, the victim line or the meaning of the dream line. Gabe Simon's view is not heard. All transcript readings are tool-extracted, and nothing was checked against the recording.

title: People Watching
lyric_access: partial: sung excerpts printed in the Song Exploder 298 transcript (SS-S1, tool extract): an 8-line chorus, the 10-line demo version of verse 1, the 3-line discarded chorus from the Sleeper Sounds demo, a 3-line vigil passage leading into the chorus, a 2-line middle eight, and the final section (one new couplet, then the chorus repeated). Not seen: verse 2, which press describes as the state of the care home (SS-S11, SS-S3). The released verse 1 is known only through NME's description, which matches the demo. The transcript does not label sections, so section names are inferred. No official lyric page was found, and unlicensed lyric sites were not opened.
angle: The subject label is grief for a mentor who died in a care home. The angle is what the narrator does on the walk home from her bedside: he watches strangers, and the song finds its chorus in their trouble rather than his, ending on the thought that anyone on the street is somebody's loved one. From there the grief opens into anger at his town's poverty and guilt at his own luck, and the song closes in gratitude (SS-S1). The title takes an idle pastime and makes it the way he survives the walk.
narrator: First person, and Fender himself (SS-S1). For most of the visible lyric there is no addressee: the verse and chorus are observation and memory. The friend is addressed as 'you' only late, in the vigil passage, the middle eight and the final promise (visible excerpts; text-only). The stance is numb, restless watching that becomes tenderness. Ambiguities: the people on treadmills can be literal gym-goers or the daily grind, and the town falling can be his town's decline or his own collapse. The chorus images were gathered in Los Angeles, but the song is set at home.

section_map.function: Walking home, watching people gives a small spark and relief from loneliness and from himself. Then a memory of youthful invincibility and shouting along at a local venue, which now darkens him. NME's description of the released verse matches.

A run of observed strangers: people on treadmills, people sheltering from the heat under billboards, someone's loved one on the street tonight. The narrator can't stop running and watches the whole town fall. Closes on the title refrain, repeated.
The state of the care home. NME calls it the most biting section; Wikipedia's summary of Neon Music says it criticises an understaffed healthcare system.
One line of staying up all night while she died, which he calls love, then straight back to watching people on the walk home. Section label inferred.
Written last, as a parting tribute: a memorial garden in the rain, birds tracing her initials in the sky. Addressed to her.
Fear for the state of the country, a promise to hold her in his heart until he dies, then the chorus repeated with backing vocals, ending on a tenor sax solo.

title_hook: The title names the narrator's activity. It opens the demo verse and closes every chorus as a repeated refrain, so the song starts and resolves on it. The phrase is a mild everyday pastime that takes its weight from where he is walking home from, and the chorus reveals what he is actually watching. It is also the album title. Sound and placement on the beat: text-only, not checked against the recording.

language_choices.what_it_does: From Fender's memory of a Billy Connolly programme about a Scottish grave marked 'Somebody's Sweetheart'. In two words a stranger sleeping rough becomes someone's loved one, and the private grief becomes empathy for strangers.
Plain description that also reads as the rat race; the narrator who 'can't stop running' is then one of them.
Street imagery from the Hollywood Boulevard drive placed inside a song set in North Shields, which makes the chorus placeless: these could be strangers anywhere.

language_choices.choice: the vigil line that calls an all-night watch love
language_choices.what_it_does: The plainest statement in the song. It gets one line, and then the song is back on the walk home, so it never lingers in the room.
The one openly fanciful image, saved for the farewell section. It stands out against Fender's stated preference for plain description (SS-S5).

language_choices.choice: the discarded chorus's line about debt
language_choices.what_it_does: Stated the town's poverty outright as a summary. In the released song the politics arrives through images (a loved one on the street) and verse 2's care home instead.

connective_lines: The demo verse's middle lines plainly explain why he watches (relief from loneliness, from himself), which makes the title activity motivated rather than decorative. The vigil line is the hinge between private and public: one line at the deathbed, and the next line is back on the walk home. Text-only; verse 2 not seen.
musical: Writer statements (SS-S1): it began as a chord progression on a battered school piano with pin tacks added for a metallic, honky-tonk sound. His demos are phone loops (drums, piano, bass), and he usually finds lyric and melody once a loop is running. He chose a celebratory, euphoric, liberating feel over a slower ballad to reach the acceptance stage of grief. A straight drum beat was played at Granduciel's request, with toms overdubbed. The Wurlitzer riff was doubled by a Knopfler-style picked guitar because it didn't cut through, and a single OB-8 synth preset sits above the melody. Fender and Granduciel played the acoustic guitars live as a one-take duet on a binaural head mic. Johnny 'Bluehat' Davis played the tenor sax outro solo in one take. Brooke Bentham sang harmonies on the choruses. Rosie Danvers arranged 30-piece strings, recorded at Abbey Road Studio Two. Fender recorded his vocals at home. Press (SS-S11): driving, expansive, cinematic heartland rock, 5:11. Text-only boundary: no claim about melody, stress, or how the title sits rhythmically.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Fender
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The song is for Annie Orwin, an actor who ran the community acting class he joined at about 13, gave him confidence after he was bullied, and first convinced him music could be a career; she died after a five-day vigil.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Fender
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The people-watching idea came on walks home from the care home; watching strangers was an escape that led to thoughts of mortality, the cost-of-living crisis, and guilt at his success while people at home struggled.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Fender
writer_commentary.paraphrase: He wanted the liberation of grief's acceptance phase rather than a slow ballad: something celebratory and euphoric for a larger-than-life person.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Fender
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The original chorus didn't work, and because the song was about Annie it had to be right, so it sat as half a song for months; the hardest song he has written.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Fender
writer_commentary.paraphrase: In LA, the people sleeping rough on Hollywood Boulevard and a remembered grave marked 'Somebody's Sweetheart' gave him the chorus, which then came quickly on acoustic guitar; he likes the idea that everyone is loved by someone.

writer_commentary.speaker: Sam Fender
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The middle eight came last, as a final tribute; the first half is grief written while drinking heavily, and the song turns to gratitude, which he sees as where grief ends up.

writer_commentary.speaker: Joe Atkinson
writer_commentary.paraphrase: The band heard the phone demo at Sleeper Sounds and loved it immediately; Fender adds that the grief was still raw and they had all lost people.

analyst_inference: The rewrite moved the chorus from explanation to observation. The discarded chorus told the listener what the town and tragedy had done to the narrator; the kept one shows strangers and lets one line (watching the town fall) carry the verdict.

A listener hearing only the chorus would not know anyone had died. That breaks the usual test that a chorus should tell the whole song (C43): the death lives in the verse, the vigil line and the middle eight, and the chorus is what grief makes him notice.
Withholding 'you' until late makes the address the turn: after a song of watching other people, speaking to her is the first time he stops watching. (Partial lyric; text-only.)
The euphoric setting does not contradict the lyric because the lyric ends in gratitude: the music is set to where the song arrives, not where it starts.
revisions: Documented in SS-S1: (1) The original chorus, played on air from the Sleeper Sounds demo (a first-person summary of the town's debt, unforgettable streets and tragedy shaping him), was replaced several months later by a chorus written on acoustic guitar in LA, after a drive down Hollywood Boulevard and the memory of the 'Somebody's Sweetheart' grave. (2) The demo verse appears to have survived: NME's description of the released first verse (SS-S11) matches the demo excerpt. (3) The middle eight was written after everything else. (4) Arrangement: the Wurlitzer riff was doubled on guitar because it didn't cut through, and the synth and strings were added late. No other line-level drafts are documented.

transferable.craft: When a chorus about your own loss keeps failing, write what you see other people doing on the way home, with one borrowed phrase or inscription that names a stranger as loved. Keep the private loss in the verse and the late sections.
transferable.limits: Needs a verse that sets the private stakes first, or the chorus reads as detached social comment. Wrong for a song whose point is the private detail: Kahan's chorus is where his local facts live.

transferable.craft: Set the music to the stage the lyric ends at (acceptance, gratitude) rather than to the subject.
transferable.limits: Writer statement, not checked by listening. If the words never arrive at acceptance, an uplifting setting reads as denial.

transferable.craft: Hold the second person back until late, so the address itself is the turn.
